intro: Three modules follow the AZ-900 skills measured: cloud concepts, Azure architecture and services, and management and governance.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Study guide for Exam AZ-900

modules.title: Describe cloud concepts
modules.summary: Cloud computing, shared responsibility, deployment models and service types, and the consumption-based model.

guide.html: About 25–30% of AZ-900. It tests the vocabulary of cloud computing: why organizations move to the cloud, what they pay for, and who is responsible for what.

Public cloud is owned by a provider and shared by many customers. Private cloud serves one organization. Hybrid mixes cloud and on-premises. The three service types are IaaS (you manage the OS and up, such as virtual machines), PaaS (the provider manages the platform, such as App Service) and SaaS (you just use the software, such as Microsoft 365). Serverless runs code without you managing servers, billed per execution.

The provider always owns the physical datacenter, hosts and network. You always own your data, identities and devices. Everything in between shifts with the service type: with IaaS you patch the operating system, with PaaS the provider does, and with SaaS you mostly manage data and access.

On-premises hardware is capital expenditure (CapEx), paid up front. Cloud is operational expenditure (OpEx), pay as you go. Benefits tested: high availability, scalability (scale up/out), elasticity (scale automatically with demand), reliability, predictability, security, governance and manageability. A consumption-based model charges only for what you use.

tips: Scale up adds power to one machine; scale out adds more machines.
Data is always the customer's responsibility.
Hybrid cloud is public plus private or on-premises, not just two public clouds.
terms: Rent virtual infrastructure; you manage the OS and applications.
The provider manages the platform; you manage the app and data.
Finished software delivered over the internet.
Automatically adding or removing resources as demand changes.

modules.title: Describe Azure architecture and services
modules.summary: Regions, availability zones, resource hierarchy, compute, networking, storage, identity and security.

guide.html: The biggest domain at 35–40%. Know the building blocks of Azure and which service fits a need.

A region is a set of datacenters in one geography. Availability zones are separate datacenters inside a region, protecting against datacenter failure. A region pair is a second region in the same geography for disaster recovery. Resources live in resource groups inside subscriptions, which sit under management groups.

Virtual Machines give full OS control. Virtual Machine Scale Sets add or remove identical VMs automatically. App Service hosts web apps without servers to manage. Azure Functions run event-driven serverless code. Containers use Container Instances (simple) or Kubernetes Service (orchestrated). A virtual network connects resources privately; VPN Gateway and ExpressRoute connect on-premises (ExpressRoute is a private, dedicated link). Azure DNS hosts domains.

Storage account services: Blob (objects), Files (SMB shares), Queue (messages), Table (NoSQL). Redundancy options: LRS, ZRS, GRS, GZRS. Access tiers are hot, cool, cold and archive. Microsoft Entra ID is the cloud identity service, with single sign-on, MFA, Conditional Access and passwordless options. Zero Trust means never trust, always verify. Defense in depth layers protections.

tips: Availability zones protect within a region; region pairs protect across regions.
Archive is the cheapest tier but needs hours to rehydrate.
ExpressRoute does not use the public internet.
terms: A physically separate datacenter within a region.
A logical container for related resources.
A private dedicated connection to Azure.
Microsoft's cloud identity and access service.

modules.title: Describe Azure management and governance
modules.summary: Cost management, governance and compliance tools, and the tools for deploying and monitoring resources.

guide.html: About 30–35%. Cost tools, governance features, and how you manage Azure.

Factors that affect cost: resource type, consumption, region, bandwidth and subscription type. The Pricing calculator estimates new workloads; the Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) calculator compares on-premises to Azure; Cost Management tracks and budgets real spending; tags label resources for cost reporting. Reservations and savings plans lower cost for committed use.

Azure Policy enforces rules (for example allowed regions). Resource locks prevent deletion (CanNotDelete) or change (ReadOnly). Role-based access control (RBAC) grants permissions. Microsoft Purview supports data governance and compliance; Service Trust Portal publishes compliance documents. Azure Blueprints-style patterns have been replaced by template specs and deployment stacks.

Use the Azure portal (web), Azure CLI and PowerShell (command line), Cloud Shell (browser terminal), and ARM templates or Bicep (infrastructure as code). Azure Arc extends management to on-premises and other clouds. Azure Monitor collects metrics and logs; Azure Advisor gives recommendations; Service Health reports Azure incidents affecting you.

tips: Policy says what is allowed; RBAC says who can act; locks stop accidents.
Pricing calculator = new Azure estimates; TCO = compare with on-premises.
terms: Evaluates and enforces rules on resources.
A name/value label on a resource.
Tracks, analyzes and budgets Azure spending.
Extends Azure management to other environments.
A declarative language for deploying Azure resources.
